title: Validate the source path and discover hosts
clue: No response, a new subnet, or uncertainty about the interface and route
conditions: Correct VPN/interface and explicit scope; discovery probes must be compatible with the path
access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position
result: A source-qualified reachable-host list and a defensible discovery limitation
mechanics: Discovery probes identify responders; silence can be caused by filtering. A known assigned host can still require a port scan that skips discovery.
checks:
```bash
ip addr
ip route get TARGET
nmap -sn SUBNET -oA host-discovery
```
example: Observation: a known host is absent from the ping sweep. Test: confirm the route and scan its selected application port with discovery skipped. Illustrative output: TCP/443 is open. Interpretation: discovery missed a live service; retain the host and enumerate HTTPS.
verify: Record source address/interface, route and the exact responding endpoint; a missing ping response does not prove a host is down.
failure: No route or wrong VPN interface is an environment failure. If only discovery is blocked, use the known-host TCP method; a SOCKS path requires a compatible connect-based client.

recognition.where: From the assessment host inspect the assigned interface and the route to the exact target before interpreting silence.
recognition.commands:
```bash
ip addr
ip route get TARGET
nmap -sn SUBNET -oA host-discovery
```
recognition.sample:
TARGET via VPN_GATEWAY dev tun0 src SOURCE_IP
Nmap scan report for HOSTNAME (TARGET)
Host is up
recognition.spot: The route names the intended interface/source; a responder is evidence from that source, not a global reachability claim.
recognition.confirm: Check scope, target state and whether host-discovery probes are permitted by this path.
recognition.enabled: The assigned route is correct and the selected application responds: proceed to service coverage.
recognition.ruledout: The route points outside the assigned VPN: repair that route before evaluating the target.
recognition.unknown: No discovery response but a plausible route exists: the host may filter probes; test a justified selected port.

> **Purpose:** Confirm the source path and discover explicitly assigned hosts before spending time on port coverage. ##### 1. Check the path From the target's working folder: ```bash mkdir -p scans ip -br addr ip route get TARGET ``` > **Read:** selected interface/source address. A route lookup does not prove reachability.
Variants — discover one host, a host list or a subnet ##### Host discovery **One host:** ```bash nmap -sn -n -oA scans/host TARGET ``` **Assigned list:** put IPs in `targets.txt`, one per line. ```bash nmap -sn -n -iL targets.txt -oA scans/hosts ``` **Explicitly assigned subnet:** ```bash nmap -sn -n -oA scans/subnet SUBNET ``` No response does not establish that a host is offline. A list of assigned hosts does not imply the surrounding subnet is in scope.

title: Discover TCP ports with SYN or connect scans
clue: An assigned host needs an initial service queue or full TCP coverage
conditions: SYN scanning needs raw-packet privileges; connect scanning needs OS TCP connections; specify selected versus full port coverage
access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position
result: A saved TCP port-state inventory with explicit coverage
mechanics: SYN and connect scans infer reachability differently but both cover only their selected ports. A common-port scan is a prioritization pass, not full TCP coverage.
checks:
```bash
nmap -Pn -sT --top-ports 1000 TARGET -oA tcp-initial
nmap -Pn -sT -p- TARGET -oA tcp-full
```
example: Observation: the initial scan exposes SSH and HTTP. Test: finish full TCP selection. Illustrative output: an additional management service appears on a high port. Interpretation: add it to the queue before committing to a web-only path.
verify: Retain the selected port set, source context, completion/errors and raw output; follow open ports with focused application evidence.
failure: Filtered is not closed. Through SOCKS use supported TCP-connect behavior and skip unsupported raw discovery/UDP; if results conflict, compare from the actual source.

recognition.where: After path validation, compare a first TCP pass with explicit full-port coverage; record skipped discovery or privilege limitations.
recognition.commands:
```bash
nmap -Pn -sT --top-ports 1000 TARGET -oA tcp-initial
nmap -Pn -sT -p- TARGET -oA tcp-full
```
recognition.sample:
Initial selection: 22/tcp open ssh; 80/tcp open http
Full selection also: 18080/tcp open unknown
recognition.spot: The high listener exists outside the first selection; its application label remains provisional.
recognition.confirm: Confirm scan completion, source, errors and application behavior on each interesting port.
recognition.enabled: A focused connection and application response confirm the listener: queue its service.
recognition.ruledout: The earlier result cannot be reproduced after a completed focused check: retire that stale listener hypothesis.
recognition.unknown: Filtered ports or interrupted scans leave coverage/reachability unresolved; save the limit and choose a focused check.

procedure:
> **Purpose:** Get quick leads, complete TCP coverage, and adapt scan type, discovery handling, timing and output to the access path. ##### 2. Get initial TCP results ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -oA scans/tcp-initial TARGET ``` > **Coverage:** 1,000 common TCP ports. Review `scans/tcp-initial.nmap` in a text editor.
Variants — host list, connect scan or selected ports ##### Initial view: 1,000 common ports **Assigned host list, SYN scan:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -iL targets.txt -oA scans/tcp-initial-list ``` **One host, connect scan without raw-packet privileges:** ```bash nmap -sT -n -oA scans/tcp-connect TARGET ``` Default coverage is the common-port selection, not ports 1-1000. ##### Selected ports or a range **One host:** replace PORTS with, for example, `25,43` or `1-1024`. ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-selected TARGET ``` **Find relevant services across assigned hosts:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p PORTS -iL targets.txt -oA scans/tcp-service-sweep ``` A focused service sweep is not a full port map.
##### 3. Complete TCP coverage ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -oA scans/tcp-all TARGET ``` > **Coverage:** TCP 1-65535. Investigate useful initial results while this runs.
Variants — connect scan, blocked discovery, timing and progress ##### All TCP ports: 1-65535 **Connect scan:** ```bash nmap -sT -n -p- -oA scans/tcp-all-connect TARGET ``` Inspect additional endpoints before narrowing the investigation. TCP coverage says nothing about UDP. ##### Discovery skips a running target **Recheck relevant ports with response reasons:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -Pn --reason -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-recheck TARGET ``` **Proceed with full TCP coverage despite failed discovery:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -Pn -p- -oA scans/tcp-all-no-discovery TARGET ``` `-Pn` assumes online status; inspect actual responses. It does not fix routing. Use `-sT` without sudo if ordinary TCP connections are needed. ##### Timing and progress **Full TCP with normal timing and periodic progress:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -T3 --stats-every 30s -oA scans/tcp-normal TARGET ``` **Faster timing on a stable path:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -p- -T4 --stats-every 30s -oA scans/tcp-faster TARGET ``` `-T3` is normal timing; `-T4` is more aggressive. Periodic progress changes display, not coverage. Recheck decisive results if loss or filtering makes observations uncertain. ##### TCP-only access through a SOCKS proxy Use ordinary connect calls when a previously established proxy is the only route. This is a bounded first view, not complete TCP coverage: ```bash proxychains nmap -sT -Pn -n --top-ports 100 -oA scans/tcp-proxy-top100 TARGET ``` `proxychains` cannot turn SYN probes or UDP into proxied TCP connections. `-Pn` avoids discovery probes that may not traverse the proxy. Confirm the proxy route first, preserve the 100-port limit, and expand with another connect scan only when scope and path permit it.

title: Identify applications and validate selected NSE checks
clue: A listener has a port-based label or uncertain version
conditions: A reachable selected port; scripts must match the application and permitted assessment behavior
access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position
result: Application and version evidence sufficient to choose service enumeration or an exploit candidate
mechanics: Port numbers and banners suggest a protocol; application responses and exact configuration constrain an exploit. NSE results remain candidates when the check cannot prove the vulnerable condition.
checks:
```bash
nmap -Pn -sV -p PORTS TARGET -oA selected-services
nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME
```
example: Observation: port 8443 is labelled HTTPS but the product is unknown. Test: version probes and a normal HTTP request. Illustrative output: a named management product and login route. Interpretation: map authentication and verify the build before exploit selection.
verify: Preserve the responding product/version evidence and distinguish an inferred fingerprint from a confirmed vulnerable build.
failure: A timeout, generic banner or scanner label leaves identity inconclusive; use native protocol clients or the unknown-port method.

recognition.where: Take the discovered open-port list and request protocol/version evidence rather than choosing attacks from conventional port numbers.
recognition.sample:
18080/tcp open http APPLICATION_SERVER
Service detection performed
recognition.spot: An HTTP response on a nonstandard port routes investigation to application mapping; a product string is still only fingerprint evidence.
recognition.confirm: Verify normal requests, hostname/TLS requirements and exact build/configuration before selecting an exploit.
recognition.enabled: Native protocol responses agree with the fingerprint: use that service's enumeration guide.
recognition.ruledout: A presumed SSH port instead speaks HTTP: discard the SSH-specific method for that endpoint.
recognition.unknown: Generic banners or timeouts do not identify a build; try protocol-aware/TLS discrimination.

procedure:
> **Purpose:** Identify applications on discovered ports and choose only the probing needed for the next decision. ##### 4. Identify discovered applications ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services TARGET ``` > **Next:** choose service-specific enumeration from application evidence. A version match alone does not establish exploitability.
Variants — default scripts, named scripts and OS fingerprints ##### Identify applications on discovered ports **Version probing plus the default NSE script set:** use when those scripts answer relevant enumeration questions. ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV -sC -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services-default TARGET ``` Read the application evidence and script results. Default scripts add interactions; they do not complete service enumeration or prove exploitability. **Lighter version probing when time or fragile service behavior matters:** ```bash nmap -sT -n -sV --version-light -p PORTS -oA scans/tcp-services-light TARGET ``` Light mode tries fewer uncommon probes and can miss an identity that the default intensity finds. Use the default first unless a concrete constraint justifies the tradeoff. ##### Select a named script **Inspect behavior locally:** ```bash nmap --script-help http-headers ``` **After identifying HTTP, inspect its relevant port(s):** ```bash nmap -sT -n -p PORTS --script http-headers -oA scans/http-headers TARGET ``` Returned headers are clues. Choose scripts for the question they answer and their behavior. ##### OS fingerprinting and bundled probing **Estimate OS from network-stack behavior:** ```bash sudo nmap -n -O -oA scans/os TARGET ``` **Request more tentative OS guesses:** ```bash sudo nmap -n -O --osscan-guess -oA scans/os-guesses TARGET ``` **Bundle OS/version detection, default scripts and traceroute:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -A -oA scans/combined-detail TARGET ``` OS guesses are hypotheses. These use default TCP coverage; `-A` does not mean all ports. Choose this bundle only when its additional probing is useful.

title: Probe UDP and resolve ambiguous silence
clue: TCP enumeration is incomplete for the objective or DNS/SNMP/RPC clues suggest UDP
conditions: Raw-packet access and UDP reachability from the real source; bounded or full selection must be explicit
access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position
result: UDP responders and documented open/filtered uncertainty
mechanics: A UDP service may ignore an empty probe; ICMP errors and application responses distinguish states. Silence alone cannot distinguish open from filtered.
checks:
```bash
sudo nmap -Pn -sU --top-ports 20 --reason TARGET -oA udp-initial
sudo nmap -Pn -sU -sV -p 53,161 TARGET -oA udp-focused
```
example: Observation: UDP/161 is open|filtered. Test: a correctly formatted SNMP request with a justified community. Illustrative output: system OIDs return. Interpretation: SNMP is confirmed accessible; enumerate useful branches.
verify: Use an application response for a confirmed service; document unresolved silence, coverage and ICMP rate-limit effects.
failure: Do not translate UDP silence into a closed service. Retry a focused application-aware probe or a different permitted vantage point.

recognition.where: Inspect discovery results and DNS/SNMP/RPC clues, then probe a separate bounded UDP selection from the same source.
recognition.sample:
161/udp open|filtered snmp no-response
53/udp open domain udp-response
recognition.spot: A DNS response confirms a UDP application; open|filtered SNMP silence is a candidate requiring a correctly formatted request.
recognition.confirm: Check accepted service parameters, response identity and possible ICMP rate limiting.
recognition.enabled: A service-native request returns the expected OID/record: enumerate that application.
recognition.ruledout: An explicit port-unreachable response rules out that UDP endpoint for this source/time.
recognition.unknown: Silence can mean open or filtered; use a justified application-aware probe rather than declaring either.

procedure:

procedure:
> **Purpose:** Resolve uncertainty that affects a decision, preserve coverage limits, and turn scan output into a service-enumeration queue. ##### 6. Resolve a result that changes your next action Keep source, destination, transport and port consistent when comparing results. Revisit relevant checks after a new route, foothold or identity changes access.
Variants — Netcat verification, response reasons and readable output ##### Netcat connection check **One TCP port:** replace PORTS with one number. ```bash nc -nv -w 3 -z TARGET PORTS ``` **Short port range:** replace PORTS with a range such as `3388-3390`. ```bash nc -nvv -w 3 -z TARGET PORTS ``` Success establishes TCP connection acceptance; refusal and timeout differ. The second form gives more verbose output. A three-second wait may be insufficient on a slow path. ##### Output and diagnostics **Readable text only, with verbose output and port-state reasons:** ```bash sudo nmap -sS -n -v --reason -p PORTS -oN scans/tcp-check.txt TARGET ``` Open saved `.nmap` or `.txt` output in a text editor. `-oA` writes `.nmap`, `.gnmap` and `.xml`; `-oN` writes only normal text. Use a different output prefix when retaining another run.
##### 7. Build the service queue Open the saved `.nmap` files in a text editor. For every useful endpoint, capture one line with this structure: ```text SOURCE -> TARGET | tcp/udp PORT | OBSERVED STATE | APPLICATION EVIDENCE | COVERAGE LIMIT | NEXT TEST ``` > **Next:** carry the complete endpoint tuple into [Stage 02 service enumeration](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/02-service-enumeration/README.md) and choose the cheapest protocol-aware test that can change your understanding or access. Keep an explicit return item for incomplete TCP, UDP or application coverage.
Interpretation cues — preserve what the scan actually established - `open` establishes a reachable endpoint from the scan source; it does not establish a vulnerability or usable authentication. - `closed` records an explicit rejection in that context. Move on unless later evidence changes the route, source or target state. - `filtered` leaves the listener state unresolved because filtering, loss or the path prevented classification. - `unfiltered` means the selected probe reached the port but could not determine whether it was open or closed; use a scan type that can answer the required question. - UDP `open|filtered` is inconclusive. A useful protocol probe may reduce uncertainty, but another silence can remain inconclusive. - `closed|filtered` is also an explicit ambiguity. Preserve it unless resolving the distinction changes the next action. - A port-based service label is a clue. Use application evidence before treating product, version, operating system or machine role as confirmed. - Record the exact target, transport, selected ports and source position. A successful narrow scan does not cover untested ports, the other transport or another network position.
##### 8. Prioritize and know when to rescan Rank candidates by the cheapest test likely to produce access, credentials, sensitive information or a decisive prerequisite. Prefer observed application behavior over conventional port numbers. Keep at least one return item for incomplete coverage so an attractive early service does not erase the rest of the map. Re-run network discovery after a new source host, route, tunnel or target restart. Re-enumerate a service after a new credential or identity. Inspect local listeners after a foothold. Recheck a previous result when the source, target state, port selection or network conditions changed—not simply because the first attack failed.

clue: The useful vantage point is a Windows host without Nmap
conditions: A permitted Windows shell, explicit target list and built-in networking support
access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position
result: Selected TCP reachability from the Windows network position
mechanics: A local TcpClient or Test-NetConnection uses the host's route and firewall context. Results from Kali do not substitute for reachability from this source.

example: Observation: Kali cannot reach an internal WinRM endpoint. Test: check TCP/5985 from the Windows foothold. Illustrative output: TcpTestSucceeded is True. Interpretation: a new route/source exists; choose a forward or run an authorized native client there.

title: Discriminate unknown listeners and use scanner alternatives
clue: A nonstandard listener, slow TCP discovery or a scanner-specific candidate
conditions: Explicit bounded scope; raw scanning alternatives need their required privileges and conservative rates
access: An explicitly assigned address or host list and a known source position
result: A validated listener/protocol candidate rather than an unverified scanner finding
mechanics: Fast discovery tools trade probing depth for speed. Recheck discovered ports with Nmap and a native client; a vulnerability-script label is not a complete exploit proof.
checks:
```bash
nmap -Pn -sV --version-all -p PORT TARGET
nc -nv TARGET PORT
```
example: Observation: fast discovery reports an unexpected high port. Test: a focused version probe and protocol request. Illustrative output: an HTTP response appears. Interpretation: treat it as a web application regardless of its port.
verify: Confirm the endpoint through independent application behavior and preserve the rate/scope used for discovery.
failure: No response may require TLS or a protocol-first request. Avoid treating speed-oriented results as complete, and keep prohibited mass vulnerability scanners outside the exam path.

recognition.where: Select an unexplained listener from the saved queue, compare native connection behavior, then use focused version/TLS probes.
recognition.commands:
```bash
nmap -Pn -sV --version-all -p PORT TARGET
nc -nv TARGET PORT
```
recognition.sample:
PORT/tcp open ssl/http APPLICATION
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://HOSTNAME/
recognition.spot: TLS and an HTTP redirect suggest a hostname-selected web application rather than an attack tied to the port number.
recognition.confirm: Reproduce the hostname/TLS request and confirm exact software/configuration.
recognition.enabled: A correctly addressed request produces the application: move to its normal behavior map.
recognition.ruledout: The banner disproves the originally assumed protocol: remove that service hypothesis.
recognition.unknown: No banner may mean a client-first protocol, TLS or filtering; use a discriminating normal request.

procedure:
> **Use when:** Nmap remains the interpretation baseline, but a faster TCP discovery pass or a bounded web-server check is useful. These tools generate candidates; Nmap/manual protocol checks confirm them. ##### RustScan: fast TCP discovery, Nmap interpretation > **Prerequisite:** RustScan and Nmap on Kali; direct TCP reachability. **Coverage:** only the explicit TCP range. **Decisive output:** a discovered port that Nmap can reproduce and identify. ```bash rustscan -a TARGET -r 1-65535 --ulimit 5000 -- \ -Pn -sV -sC -oA rustscan-followup ``` If the target or network becomes unstable, lower concurrency rather than trusting an empty result. RustScan does not replace UDP work and does not prove that closed/filtered ports were tested with the same semantics as Nmap.
Bounded first 1,000 TCP ports ```bash rustscan -a TARGET -r 1-1000 --ulimit 5000 -- \ -Pn -sV -sC -oA rustscan-1000 ``` > Use only for a quick selection. It is not full TCP coverage and is not equivalent to Nmap's default top-1,000 selection.
##### Masscan: raw-packet discovery, then validation > **Prerequisite:** root/raw-packet access and a directly routed target. **Choose it:** for a large authorized address/port space where discovery speed matters. **Failure cue:** high loss or inconsistent results at the chosen rate. ```bash sudo masscan TARGET -p1-65535 --rate 500 -oL masscan-open.txt ``` Treat each hit as a candidate and recheck with Nmap: ```bash PORTS=$(awk '$1 == "open" && $2 == "tcp" {print $3}' masscan-open.txt \ | sort -nu | paste -sd,) test -n "$PORTS" && sudo nmap -Pn -sV -sC -p "$PORTS" TARGET -oA masscan-verified ``` Masscan's raw-packet model is not suitable through a TCP SOCKS proxy. A rate that overwhelms the path can create false negatives and disrupt the lab; record the rate with the result. ##### Unknown-port discrimination Start passively or with protocol-appropriate probes. Do not spray arbitrary strings at a stateful or destructive service. ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --version-all -p PORT TARGET -oN port-PORT-version.txt nmap --script-help banner nmap -Pn --script=banner -p PORT TARGET -oN port-PORT-banner.txt nc -nv TARGET PORT openssl s_client -connect TARGET:PORT -servername HOSTNAME curl -vk --max-time 10 https://TARGET:PORT/ ``` > **Next action:** route application evidence to the matching Stage 02 page. If TLS succeeds but HTTP does not, preserve the certificate names and protocol evidence instead of labelling it HTTPS. ##### NSE candidate checks Inspect a script before selecting it: ```bash nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME grep -i 'SCRIPT_NAME' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/script.db ``` Run a named script against a confirmed service/port: ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script SCRIPT_NAME -p PORT TARGET -oN nse-SCRIPT_NAME.txt ``` The broad `vuln` category is candidate generation and can be intrusive or misleading. If its use is justified in the authorized lab, restrict it to identified ports and manually validate every result: ```bash nmap -Pn -sV --script vuln -p PORTS TARGET -oN nse-vuln-candidates.txt ``` Avoid `*brute*` categories as a default; first establish exact service, known test identities, lockout/rate limits and explicit authorization. ##### Nikto: bounded web-server candidate generation > **Prerequisite:** an identified HTTP(S) endpoint. **Choose it:** after manual baselining to identify common files, headers and server misconfiguration candidates. **Decisive output:** a finding manually reproduced with the same host, path and authentication context. ```bash nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -output nikto-TARGET-PORT.txt ```
HTTPS, host name and tuning variants ```bash nikto -h https://HOSTNAME:PORT -output nikto-HOSTNAME-PORT.txt nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -vhost HOSTNAME -output nikto-vhost.txt nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -Tuning 123b -output nikto-focused.txt ``` > Tuning codes are version-sensitive. Inspect `nikto -H` / local documentation before relying on a copied code set.

html.procedure:
RustScan: fast TCP discovery, Nmap interpretation

Prerequisite: RustScan and Nmap on Kali; direct TCP reachability. Coverage: only the explicit TCP range. Decisive output: a discovered port that Nmap can reproduce and identify.

# RustScan: fast TCP discovery, Nmap interpretation
rustscan -a TARGET -r 1-65535 --ulimit 5000 -- \
  -Pn -sV -sC -oA rustscan-followup

# Bounded first 1,000 TCP ports
rustscan -a TARGET -r 1-1000 --ulimit 5000 -- \
  -Pn -sV -sC -oA rustscan-1000

Masscan: raw-packet discovery, then validation

Use only for a quick selection. It is not full TCP coverage and is not equivalent to Nmap's default top-1,000 selection.

Prerequisite: root/raw-packet access and a directly routed target. Choose it: for a large authorized address/port space where discovery speed matters. Failure cue: high loss or inconsistent results at the chosen rate.

# Masscan: raw-packet discovery, then validation
sudo masscan TARGET -p1-65535 --rate 500 -oL masscan-open.txt

# Treat each hit as a candidate and recheck with Nmap
PORTS=$(awk '$1 == "open" && $2 == "tcp" {print $3}' masscan-open.txt \
  | sort -nu | paste -sd,)
test -n "$PORTS" && sudo nmap -Pn -sV -sC -p "$PORTS" TARGET -oA masscan-verified

# Unknown-port discrimination
nmap -Pn -sV --version-all -p PORT TARGET -oN port-PORT-version.txt
nmap --script-help banner
nmap -Pn --script=banner -p PORT TARGET -oN port-PORT-banner.txt
nc -nv TARGET PORT
openssl s_client -connect TARGET:PORT -servername HOSTNAME
curl -vk --max-time 10 https://TARGET:PORT/

Inspect a script before selecting it

# Inspect a script before selecting it
nmap --script-help SCRIPT_NAME
grep -i 'SCRIPT_NAME' /usr/share/nmap/scripts/script.db

# Run a named script against a confirmed service/port
nmap -Pn -sV --script SCRIPT_NAME -p PORT TARGET -oN nse-SCRIPT_NAME.txt

# NSE candidate checks
nmap -Pn -sV --script vuln -p PORTS TARGET -oN nse-vuln-candidates.txt

Nikto: bounded web-server candidate generation

Prerequisite: an identified HTTP(S) endpoint. Choose it: after manual baselining to identify common files, headers and server misconfiguration candidates. Decisive output: a finding manually reproduced with the same host, path and authentication context.

# Nikto: bounded web-server candidate generation
nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -output nikto-TARGET-PORT.txt

# HTTPS, host name and tuning variants
nikto -h https://HOSTNAME:PORT -output nikto-HOSTNAME-PORT.txt
nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -vhost HOSTNAME -output nikto-vhost.txt
nikto -h http://TARGET:PORT -Tuning 123b -output nikto-focused.txt

Tuning codes are version-sensitive. Inspect nikto -H / local documentation before relying on a copied code set.

Nikto is explicitly listed as allowed by the current OffSec exam guide, but its findings remain scanner candidates. Recheck the guide before an exam and manually validate anything that affects an attack decision.
